newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euroclear, Cedel to study banks forex clearing plan.
newsitem.headline: Euroclear, Cedel to study banks forex clearing plan.

text.p: Brussels-based Euroclear and Luxembourg's Cedel Bank, two major securities clearance and settlement houses, said on Tuesday they would be interested in examining plans for a global foreign exchange clearing system.
"We'd be seriously interested in looking at it. But a lot of water would need to pass under the bridge before we'd think about linking with this kind of idea," Euroclear spokesman Denis Peters said.
"We'd have to look carefully to see if there are synergies. But it could be that we'd look at being in business with them," Cedel spokesman John Gilchrist said.

On Tuesday the so-called Group of 20 (G20) international banks unveiled plans for a global clearing house to reduce settlement risk in the foreign exchange market which sees $1.2 trillion daily turnover.
The G20 is expected to make a final decision on the project by the end of 1996.
Euroclear's Peters said the plan was "not a competitive threat" to Euroclear. "Depending on their success, we may be interested in doing business with them," he said.

Peters said that Euroclear was focused on the clearing and settlement of equities. "We're not entertaining the idea of entering the foreign exchange business. There are a lot of players in that market and we couldn't really meet the critical mass required to operate in a global market like that," he said.

Cedel's Gilchrist welcomed the G20 initiative. "As transactions start to speed up, the need grows for effective market mechanisms to manage risk. But they have tremendous hurdles to overcome," he said.
"The group has a strong conceptual approach and clearly there are synergies with us in risk management, but it's too early to say whether we might be interested in getting involved," said Gilchrist.
The G20, formed by senior bankers in 1994, aims to set up a worldwide foreign exchange clearing system to reduce risk from currency settlement.
Its plans have attracted attention from private and central bankers following reports which show that many banks underestimate the size of their foreign exchange exposure.

Both Cedel and Euroclear have considerable back office capacity and experience in clearing third party transactions and would at least in theory be well-placed to extend the range of services offered to the currency market.
